hero.title: Open-Source TypeScript AI Agent Runtime
hero.subtitle: Open-source TypeScript runtime for AI agents that remember, adapt, and spawn new tools. Every session on the full runtime is a GMI, a Generalized Mind Instance that keeps its own persona, mood and memory and can adjust its own traits over time. Agents write their own functions mid-task and the judge approves them; managers create specialists when the static roster does not cover the task. Cognitive memory with an Ebbinghaus forgetting curve and a 7-slot working memory. 85.6% on LongMemEval-S. Apache 2.0.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Everything you need to know about AgentOS — from first install to production deployment.

whatIsAgentOS.question: What is AgentOS?
whatIsAgentOS.answer: AgentOS is an open-source TypeScript runtime for building production AI agents, developed by Frame.dev. It provides multi-agent orchestration, cognitive memory, multimodal RAG, opt-in safety guardrails (PII redaction, content moderation, grounding checks), voice pipelines, 37 channel adapters, and 13 LLM provider integrations. AgentOS also powers the AI systems behind Wilds.ai, an AI-native gaming platform. Self-hostable and free.

isOpenSource.question: Is AgentOS free and open source?
isOpenSource.answer: Yes. The runtime, the curated extensions, the guardrail packs and the curated skills are all licensed under Apache 2.0. You can use AgentOS commercially, modify it and redistribute it under that license.

llmProviders.question: What LLM providers are supported?
llmProviders.answer: AgentOS supports 13 LLM providers: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini, Groq, Together AI, Mistral, xAI (Grok), OpenRouter, Requesty, LiteLLM, Ollama, Claude Code CLI and Gemini CLI. Provider fallback chains allow automatic failover.

language.question: What programming language is AgentOS built in?
language.answer: AgentOS is written entirely in TypeScript and runs on Node.js. The npm package is @framers/agentos. It works with any TypeScript or JavaScript project.

comparison.question: How is AgentOS different from LangChain, CrewAI, or AutoGen?
comparison.answer: AgentOS is TypeScript-native (not Python), includes cognitive memory with Ebbinghaus decay curves and HEXACO personality modeling, offers opt-in guardrail packs for PII redaction, content moderation and grounding checks, provides 37 channel adapters (Discord, Telegram, Slack, email, and more), and supports 6 orchestration strategies including graph-based agent DAGs. It also ships with 88 curated skills and a capability discovery engine that puts only the relevant tools and skills in context, within a token budget per tier.

whatIsParacosm.question: What is Paracosm?
whatIsParacosm.answer: Paracosm (https://paracosm.agentos.sh) is a structured world-model simulation engine built on AgentOS. It compiles a JSON ScenarioPackage plus a HEXACO leader profile into a turn loop on a seeded, deterministic kernel, where AgentOS agents propose events, forge new JavaScript tools at runtime that AgentOS runs in node:vm with a 10-second time limit, and produce a counterfactual artifact you can fork and replay. Three modes share one schema: turn-loop civilization sims (Mars Genesis is the canonical example), batch-trajectory digital twins, and batch-point Monte-Carlo forecasts. Open-source under Apache 2.0, npm install paracosm. Live demo: https://paracosm.agentos.sh/sim. Source: https://github.com/framerslab/paracosm. Long-form launch post (why we built it, the wilds.ai vault story, the engine reference): https://agentos.sh/blog/paracosm-launch.

whatIsWildsAi.question: What is Wilds.ai?
whatIsWildsAi.answer: Wilds.ai (https://wilds.ai) is an AI-native gaming platform built on AgentOS and Paracosm. AI characters with persistent cognitive memory and HEXACO personality traits inhabit shared world models and diverge from each other based on grounded LLM-as-judge events. Players can drop into existing worlds, fork them, or compile new ones in the browser. Wilds.ai is the canonical production deployment of the AgentOS + Paracosm stack and the official community / support channel (https://wilds.ai/discord) for both projects.

whatIsWunderland.question: What is Wunderland?
whatIsWunderland.answer: Wunderland (https://wunderland.sh) is a sister project under active development that packages a batteries-included CLI plus daemon on top of the AgentOS extension and skill registries. It ships a 60-command CLI (setup, chat, rag, agency, workflows, evaluate, provenance, knowledge, marketplace, and more), a 5-tier security model (dangerous / permissive / balanced / strict / paranoid), 9 agent presets, step-up HITL authorization, and the same cognitive memory plus graph-based RAG architecture documented in the AgentOS docs. Use @framers/agentos when you want a typescript SDK to embed in your application; use Wunderland when you want a global CLI you can install with pnpm add -g wunderland and configure with a wizard. Source at github.com/jddunn/wunderland (Apache 2.0 from 0.71.0). Preview release; APIs and CLI surface may still change. Getting-started guide: https://docs.agentos.sh/wunderland.

whatIsGMI.question: What is a GMI?
whatIsGMI.answer: GMI stands for Generalized Mind Instance. It is the agent the AgentOS runtime creates for each session: it holds that session's persona (HEXACO traits), conversation history, mood and reasoning trace, runs each turn through retrieval, prompt assembly, the model call and tool calls, and can be given cognitive memory that persists across sessions. The lightweight agent() helper calls the model directly and creates no GMI unless you pass runtime: 'gmi'; gmi() and the full runtime (AgentOS.processRequest) create GMIs.

hexaco.question: What is HEXACO personality?
hexaco.answer: HEXACO is a 6-factor personality model from psychology research (Ashton & Lee, 2007). The six dimensions are Honesty-Humility, Emotionality, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, and Openness to Experience. In AgentOS, HEXACO traits shape how agents communicate and remember. agent() writes traits above 0.65 or below 0.35 into the system prompt as behavior directives. In cognitive memory, high Emotionality increases how much a memory is rewritten when it is recalled (reconsolidation), while high Conscientiousness strengthens retrieval-induced forgetting of competing memories.

cognitiveMemory.question: How does cognitive memory work?
cognitiveMemory.answer: AgentOS cognitive memory implements 8 mechanisms from cognitive science research: reconsolidation, retrieval-induced forgetting, involuntary recall, feeling-of-knowing, temporal gist extraction, schema encoding, source confidence decay, and emotion regulation. Memories decay over time following Ebbinghaus forgetting curves (Ebbinghaus, 1885), and each successful retrieval makes a memory more stable, as in spaced repetition. Working memory follows Baddeley's multi-component model (Baddeley, 2000) with 7 slots by default: high Openness adds one, high Conscientiousness removes one, and the count stays between 5 and 9. A new memory is stored as an episodic memory by default and takes a working-memory slot. When the slots are full, the least active slot gives way and its memory stays in storage. Consolidation later turns old, often-retrieved episodic memories into semantic ones.

guardrails.question: What guardrails are available?
guardrails.answer: AgentOS has six opt-in guardrail packs: PII redaction (names, emails, phone numbers, SSNs and more), ML classifiers for toxicity, threats and NSFW content, static analysis of generated code for dangerous patterns, grounding checks against source documents, topicality enforcement to keep agents on-task, and a content-policy rewriter that rewrites or blocks output that breaks your policy. Each pack is an extension you enable on the AgentOS runtime. The classifiers pack scores prompt injection only when its local model cannot load, so for known injection phrases use the built-in phrase-list guardrail.

capabilityDiscovery.question: What is the capability discovery system?
capabilityDiscovery.answer: The capability discovery engine finds tools and skills by semantic search and puts them in the prompt in three tiers, each with a hard token budget. Tier 0 keeps category summaries in context (200 tokens by default). Tier 1 adds the top 5 semantic matches for the turn (800 tokens). Tier 2 adds full schemas or SKILL.md text for the top 2 matches (2,000 tokens). A meta-tool called discover_capabilities lets agents look up available tools at runtime.

queryRouter.question: How does the QueryRouter work?
queryRouter.answer: The QueryRouter classifies each query into one of 4 tiers and retrieves to match: T0 answers from the conversation with no retrieval, T1 runs a single vector search (a keyword search when no embedding provider is configured), T2 retrieves 15 chunks, adds related chunks through graph expansion and reranks the merged set to the top 5, and T3 runs that retrieval and then, when deep research is enabled (by default when SERPER_API_KEY is set), a deep-research pass whose findings it merges in. It then answers from what it retrieved and returns the answer with its source citations.

adaptiveIntelligence.question: What is adaptive intelligence?
adaptiveIntelligence.answer: Adaptive intelligence is how AgentOS agents adjust their behavior without retraining. Five mechanisms work together: (1) Per-turn prompt assembly: a GMI's PromptEngine builds the system prompt each turn from the persona, mood, conversation history, retrieved memories and available tools. (2) Self-evaluation: with self-improvement enabled, the self_evaluate tool scores the agent's own answer and can change the session's temperature or verbosity, or adjust a trait through adapt_personality. (3) Personality-modulated memory: HEXACO traits tune the memory mechanisms; high Openness makes involuntary recall more likely, and high Conscientiousness strengthens retrieval-induced forgetting of competing memories. (4) Memory consolidation: consolidation passes prune decayed memories, merge duplicates, turn old, often-retrieved episodic memories into semantic ones and, with an LLM configured, derive insight memories from clusters. (5) QueryRouter tiers: retrieval depth follows the query, from no retrieval when the conversation already holds the answer to deep research across the corpus for the hardest ones.

emergentBehaviors.question: What are emergent behaviors?
emergentBehaviors.answer: Emergent behaviors are capabilities that agents develop at runtime rather than being explicitly programmed. AgentOS supports five forms: (1) Runtime tool forging: with emergent: true on the AgentOS runtime, agents write new tools in JavaScript through forge_tool. The EmergentCapabilityEngine runs each one in node:vm under a time limit, and an LLM judge reviews the code and its test runs before the tool is registered. (2) Self-adjusting personality: adapt_personality moves a HEXACO trait within set bounds for the running agent. With persistWithDecay and a mutation store, each change is recorded, and the stored records lose strength at most once a day, when the agent adapts. (3) Dynamic skill management: agents enable or disable skills at runtime via manage_skills, adapting their behavioral repertoire to the task at hand. (4) Composable workflow creation: agents compose registered tools into multi-step pipelines via create_workflow, building new capabilities from existing building blocks. (5) Tiered tool promotion: a forged tool starts at the session tier. After at least 5 uses with a success rate of 0.8 or higher, and approval from two LLM reviewers, it moves to the agent tier. A host can promote a tool to the shared tier with EmergentToolRegistry.promote().

llmJudge.question: Can I use an LLM as a judge instead of a human?
llmJudge.answer: Yes. AgentOS provides two complementary LLM-as-judge mechanisms. At the agency level, hitl.llmJudge() creates an approval handler that delegates decisions to an LLM. It evaluates each ApprovalRequest against configurable criteria and returns a structured decision with a confidence score. When confidence falls below the threshold, the decision escalates to a fallback handler (another hitl handler or a human). At the graph level, the humanNode() builder accepts a judge option that delegates the interrupt decision to an LLM. If the judge is confident, the graph continues without suspension. If confidence is low, execution falls through to a normal human interrupt. Both approaches support configurable model, provider, criteria, and confidence threshold. Example: hitl.llmJudge({ model: 'gpt-4o-mini', criteria: 'Is this response factually accurate?', confidenceThreshold: 0.8, fallback: hitl.cli() }).

guardrailOverride.question: Can guardrails override HITL approvals?
guardrailOverride.answer: Yes. When hitl.guardrailOverride is enabled, guardrails run after an approval decision and can still block destructive or sensitive actions. This adds a second safety layer after auto-approve, human approval, or hitl.llmJudge(). The default post-approval guardrails include code-safety and pii-redaction, and you can configure the list with hitl.postApprovalGuardrails. Disable the override only if you explicitly want the approval handler to have the final say.

install.question: How do I install AgentOS?
install.answer: Install via npm: npm install @framers/agentos. AgentOS requires Node.js 22 or higher. For the CLI tools, install the companion package: npm install -g wunderland.

voice.question: How do I add voice capabilities?
voice.answer: AgentOS runs voice through VoicePipelineOrchestrator. You give it a streaming STT session, a streaming TTS session, an endpoint detector and a barge-in handler, and it connects them to an agent session over a transport such as a WebSocket. The speech catalog lists 13 STT providers and 13 TTS providers. Of these, 11 STT providers, including Whisper (OpenAI), Deepgram and AssemblyAI, and 10 TTS providers, including ElevenLabs, OpenAI TTS and Google Cloud TTS, are available. The other five entries (Whisper.cpp, NVIDIA NeMo, Coqui XTTS, Bark and StyleTTS2) are marked unavailable, and the provider resolver skips them. Twilio, Telnyx and Plivo providers place and end phone calls.

deploy.question: How do I deploy AgentOS?
deploy.answer: AgentOS is self-hostable and runs anywhere Node.js 22 or later runs. Deploy on your own infrastructure with Docker, on cloud providers like AWS, GCP, or Azure, or use platforms like Vercel, Railway, or Fly.io. SQLite needs no setup, and the MigrationEngine moves stored data to Postgres, Qdrant, or Pinecone when you need more scale.

offline.question: Does AgentOS work offline?
offline.answer: Yes. AgentOS works fully offline when paired with Ollama for local LLM inference. Ollama provides access to open-weight models like Llama, Mistral, and Phi locally. The SQLite storage backend and in-memory vector store require no external services. The Wunderland CLI's ollama-setup command detects or installs Ollama and configures the agent to use it.

productionReady.question: Is AgentOS production-ready?
productionReady.answer: Yes. AgentOS ships opt-in guardrail packs that redact personal data, moderate content and check answers against sources, approval gates for sensitive tool calls, spend budgets that refuse a call past the cap, and circuit breakers that take a failing provider out of rotation.

compliance.question: How does AgentOS support GDPR and SOC 2 workflows?
compliance.answer: AgentOS ships a PII redaction guardrail that strips personal data before it reaches LLM providers, and self-hosted deployment so data stays on your infrastructure. Memory exports to JSON, Markdown, Obsidian or SQLite for an access request. Forgetting a memory hides it from recall and keeps its row in the database, so an erasure request needs a delete in your own storage. GDPR and SOC 2 compliance are organizational responsibilities of the deploying team, not properties of the library itself.

support.question: Is there enterprise support available?
support.answer: Yes. For production deployments, enterprise licensing, dedicated support, and custom integrations, contact the team at team@frame.dev. Enterprise support includes priority issue resolution, architecture consulting, and deployment assistance.

selfHosted.question: Can I use AgentOS with my own infrastructure?
selfHosted.answer: Absolutely. AgentOS is designed to be self-hosted from the ground up. For self-hosted deployments, your data stays on your infrastructure with SQLite, Postgres, pgvector, Qdrant, or Neo4j. If you want a managed vendor-hosted vector database instead, Pinecone is also supported. A setup helper can start a local Qdrant container with Docker.

references.title: Academic References
references.subtitle: AgentOS cognitive memory and personality systems are grounded in peer-reviewed research.

ebbinghaus.label: Ebbinghaus, H. (1885)
ebbinghaus.title: Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology.
ebbinghaus.detail: The foundational study establishing the forgetting curve. AgentOS uses Ebbinghaus decay functions for automatic memory consolidation.

baddeley.label: Baddeley, A. D. (2000)
baddeley.title: The episodic buffer: a new component of working memory?
baddeley.detail: Introduced the 4-component model of working memory. AgentOS working memory is modeled on this architecture.

hexaco.label: Ashton, M. C., & Lee, K. (2007)
hexaco.title: Empirical, theoretical, and practical advantages of the HEXACO model of personality structure.
hexaco.detail: The HEXACO model provides the 6-factor personality dimensions used in AgentOS agent identity.

louvain.label: Blondel, V. D., Guillaume, J.-L., Lambiotte, R., & Lefebvre, E. (2008)
louvain.title: Fast unfolding of communities in large networks.
louvain.detail: The Louvain algorithm is used in AgentOS GraphRAG for community detection in knowledge graphs.

hnsw.label: Malkov, Y. A., & Yashunin, D. A. (2018)
hnsw.title: Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs.
hnsw.detail: HNSW is one of 7 vector store backends supported by AgentOS for efficient similarity search.

reconsolidation.label: Nader, K., Schafe, G. E., & LeDoux, J. E. (2000)
reconsolidation.title: Fear memories require protein synthesis in the amygdala for reconsolidation after retrieval.
reconsolidation.detail: Basis for the memory reconsolidation mechanism — memories are rewritten each time they are recalled.

rif.label: Anderson, M. C., Bjork, R. A., & Bjork, E. L. (1994)
rif.title: Remembering can cause forgetting: Retrieval dynamics in long-term memory.
rif.detail: Basis for retrieval-induced forgetting — retrieving one memory suppresses related competing memories.

involuntaryRecall.label: Berntsen, D. (2010)
involuntaryRecall.title: The unbidden past: Involuntary autobiographical memories as a basic mode of remembering.
involuntaryRecall.detail: Basis for involuntary recall — contextual cues trigger spontaneous memory activation.

cognitive.title: Cognitive Memory
cognitive.subtitle: 8 memory mechanisms inspired by cognitive science research. The agent's HEXACO traits tune seven of them.

mechanismDescriptions.reconsolidation: Memories are rewritten each time they're recalled, updating with new context
mechanismDescriptions.rif: Retrieving one memory suppresses related competing memories
mechanismDescriptions.involuntaryRecall: Spontaneous memory activation triggered by contextual cues
mechanismDescriptions.fok: Metacognitive sense that an answer exists even when not immediately retrievable
mechanismDescriptions.temporalGist: Specific details fade while the gist and meaning is preserved over time
mechanismDescriptions.schemaEncoding: New information is encoded relative to existing knowledge structures
mechanismDescriptions.sourceConfidence: Certainty about where information came from decays faster than the information itself
mechanismDescriptions.emotionRegulation: Emotional valence of memories is modulated over time

research.reconsolidation: Each act of retrieval destabilizes the memory trace, allowing it to be updated with current context before re-stabilizing. Higher Emotionality amplifies the degree of rewrite, making memories more adaptive but less stable.
research.rif: Retrieving a target memory actively inhibits related competitors via lateral suppression. Higher Conscientiousness strengthens this suppression, keeping retrieval focused but increasing forgetting of peripheral associations.
research.involuntaryRecall: Contextual cues can trigger spontaneous activation of associated memories without deliberate search. Higher Openness raises the chance of an involuntary recall, producing more serendipitous connections.
research.fok: A metacognitive judgment about the likelihood of successful retrieval, even before the answer surfaces. Higher Extraversion amplifies FOK signals, making the agent more confident in its sense of 'almost knowing.'
research.temporalGist: Over time, verbatim details decay while the semantic gist is preserved through abstraction. This is the one mechanism personality does not tune.
research.schemaEncoding: New information is assimilated into existing knowledge schemas, with schema-consistent material encoded more readily. Higher Openness strengthens the encoding boost for information that violates a schema.
research.sourceConfidence: Memory for the source of information (who said it, where it was read) decays faster than the information content itself. Higher Honesty-Humility makes the agent's own inferences and reflections lose confidence faster.
research.emotionRegulation: The emotional intensity attached to memories is actively modulated during retrieval and consolidation. Higher Agreeableness increases emotional smoothing, dampening extreme valence over time for more balanced recall.

citations.reconsolidation: Nader, Schafe & LeDoux (2000). Fear memories require protein synthesis in the amygdala for reconsolidation after retrieval. Nature, 406, 722-726.
citations.rif: Anderson, Bjork & Bjork (1994). Remembering can cause forgetting: Retrieval dynamics in long-term memory. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 20, 1063-1087.
citations.involuntaryRecall: Berntsen (2010). The unbidden past: Involuntary autobiographical memories as a basic mode of remembering. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 19, 138-142.
citations.fok: Koriat (1993). How do we know that we know? The accessibility model of the feeling of knowing. Psychological Review, 100, 609-639.
citations.temporalGist: Reyna & Brainerd (1995). Fuzzy-trace theory: An interim synthesis. Learning and Individual Differences, 7, 1-75.

cognitive.ebbinghausAnnotation: Ebbinghaus found that a day after learning, about a third was still remembered. AgentOS cognitive memory applies spaced repetition and consolidation to flatten the curve.

memoryTypes.title: Four Kinds of Memory
memoryTypes.subtitle: Working memory holds the current session. Episodic traces decay along the Ebbinghaus curve, and a consolidation pass (hourly by default) summarizes clusters of them into semantic memory with an LLM. An optional observer compresses long conversations into notes.

working.name: Working Memory
working.description: Short-term slots for the current session, cleared when a new session starts.
working.detail: 7 slots; high Openness adds one, high Conscientiousness removes one

episodic.name: Episodic Memory
episodic.description: Stores conversation episodes with temporal context. Auto-decays via Ebbinghaus curve.

semantic.name: Semantic Memory
semantic.description: Long-term knowledge extracted from episodes. GraphRAG with Louvain community detection.

observational.name: Observational Memory
observational.description: Optional observer notes. Once a conversation passes a token threshold, an LLM extracts notes, then compresses and reflects on them.

embed.name: Embed

hyde.name: HyDE
hyde.description: Generates hypothetical answers to improve recall on abstract queries. Based on Gao et al. (2022).

hybrid.name: Hybrid
hybrid.description: Keyword + semantic fusion using reciprocal rank. Best of both worlds.

emergent.title: Emergent Capabilities
emergent.subtitle: Agents that forge their own tools and spawn specialist sub-agents at runtime

forging.description: Runtime Tool Forging lets an agent write a new JavaScript function mid-task, have a separate judge LLM review it, and run it before the next turn. The default executor is a node:vm sandbox with a 5 s wall clock, a static ban on eval, require, import, process and child_process, and fetch, fs and crypto only when you grant them; it measures memory without capping it and is not a security boundary. The optional QuickJSExecutor isolates the code and caps its memory. Approved tools go into a registry for reuse.
details: Composable mode: chains existing tools via pipeline steps — safe by construction
Sandbox mode: agent-written code runs under a time limit, in node:vm or QuickJS
Three lifetime tiers (session, agent, shared); automatic promotion moves a tool from session to agent, and a host can promote it to shared
Dual-judge promotion panel: safety auditor + correctness reviewer must both approve
Usage tracking with automatic tier promotion when reliability thresholds are met

synthesis.description: Agencies dynamically spawn new agents with specific personas and skills when the existing roster cannot cover a sub-task. The orchestrator identifies the capability gap, synthesises a specialist agent with tailored instructions, and merges its output back into the main workflow. Requires approval when HITL gates are configured.

loop.description: With self-improvement on, an agent gets four tools for working on itself. self_evaluate scores its replies with an LLM judge, adapt_personality shifts its HEXACO traits within a per-session budget, manage_skills turns skills on and off, and create_workflow chains tools into reusable sequences. Memory consolidation strengthens useful memories and lets irrelevant ones decay along Ebbinghaus curves.

agencySection.title: Parallel Agency
agencySection.subtitle: Teams of specialized agents work on one request together. Six built-in strategies route outputs between them: sequential, parallel, debate, review-loop, hierarchical, or graph DAG.

single-agent.name: Single Agent
single-agent.description: One agent handling the full task on its own, with no team coordination and no shared state. The baseline against which the strategies below show what an agency adds.

sequential.name: Sequential
sequential.description: Agents run one after another in a linear pipeline. Each agent receives the previous agent's output as context, forming a progressive refinement chain.

parallel.name: Parallel
parallel.description: All agents run concurrently. Their outputs are merged by a synthesis step that combines perspectives into a single coherent response.

debate.name: Debate
debate.description: Each agent takes a side and rebuts the others over several rounds. A judge then reads the transcript and gives a verdict on which side prevailed.

reviewLoop.name: Review Loop
reviewLoop.description: One agent produces output, another reviews and requests revisions. The loop continues until the reviewer approves or max rounds are reached.

review-loop.name: Review Loop
review-loop.description: One agent produces output, another reviews and requests revisions. The loop continues until the reviewer approves or max rounds are reached.

hierarchical.name: Hierarchical
hierarchical.description: A coordinator agent dispatches sub-tasks to specialist agents via tool calls. The coordinator decides which agents to invoke and in what order at runtime.

graph.name: Graph (DAG)
graph.description: Agents declare explicit dependencies via dependsOn. The orchestrator topologically sorts agents into tiers and runs each tier concurrently.

agencySection.sharedCapabilitiesScopeNote: The roster applies within one generate() call. Across session().send() turns only message history persists. See the agency API docs for memory patterns.

benchmarks.title: Memory Benchmarks with the Reader Named
benchmarks.subtitle: AgentOS runs share one dataset and one gpt-4o-2024-08-06 judge; vendor numbers are as each vendor publishes them. The 85.6% headline routes four of six question categories to gpt-5-mini, so the table also shows the run with gpt-4o answering every question.
benchmarks.highlightSCi: Per-category reader router (gpt-4o + gpt-5-mini) · 84.2% with gpt-4o alone, level with Mastra OM gpt-4o (84.23%) · $0.0090 per correct · 3.6-second median latency
benchmarks.highlightMCi: Per-category reader router, top-5 retrieval · $0.0078 per correct · the LongMemEval paper's best GPT-4o setup scores 72.0% at top-10
benchmarks.matrixIntro: AgentOS rows and the EmergenceMem Simple Fast rerun come from agentos-bench runs on the 500-question LongMemEval sets, judged by gpt-4o-2024-08-06 with the LongMemEval rubric. Vendor rows are the numbers each vendor publishes.
benchmarks.footnote: Other published LongMemEval-S scores include agentmemory 96.2% (GPT-4o reader), Mastra OM 94.9% (gpt-5-mini reader) and Supermemory 85.2% (gemini-3-pro reader). The agentos-bench leaderboard lists every row with its reader and source.
